2027-02-02.title: Mayaltho · The Entrance of our Lord into the Temple
readings: The Spirit rests on the shoot of Jesse
Christ entered the Holy Place with his own blood
2027-02-02.alt: Mayaltho, the Entrance of our Lord into the Temple (2 February), forty days after Yaldo.
2027-02-02.verse: Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation.
theo: Forty days after his birth, Mary and Joseph bring the Child to the Temple “to present him to the Lord”, as the Law required for every firstborn son, and they offer the sacrifice of the poor: “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (Leviticus 12:8). The Lord of the Temple enters his own house, carried in his mother's arms. Malachi had promised: “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple” (Malachi 3:1).

There an old man, Simeon, “righteous and devout, looking forward to the consolation of Israel”, takes the Child in his arms and praises God: “Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel.” A whole life of waiting is fulfilled in one embrace.

Then Simeon says to Mary: “This child is destined for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be opposed… and a sword will pierce your own soul too.” Joy and sorrow meet at the Temple door. The Child presented today will offer himself on the Cross. Hebrews says: Christ “entered once for all into the Holy Place, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood, thus obtaining eternal redemption.”

Mayaltho comes just before the Great Fast. It teaches us to present our lives to God, as Mary and Joseph presented Jesus; to wait faithfully like Simeon and Anna; and to welcome Christ, the light of the nations, into our arms and our hearts.
conn: The Lord comes to his Temple.
Malachi 3:1 is fulfilled: the Lord enters his Temple, not in power but as a child.
The offering of the poor.
Leviticus 12:8: the Holy Family offered two birds, the gift of those who could not afford a lamb. The true Lamb was in Mary's arms.
Without blemish.
Leviticus 22:17–25 requires offerings without blemish; Christ is the spotless offering (1 Peter 1:19; Hebrews 9:14).
Light to the nations.
Simeon's song echoes Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6: the Servant is “a light to the nations”.
altar: Simeon held the Lord in his arms; in Holy Communion we receive him into our hearts. Simeon's song is a fitting prayer after Communion: “Now, Lord, let your servant go in peace; my eyes have seen your salvation.”
outline: Forty days after Yaldo the Child comes to the Temple.
Mary and Joseph give their Son to God. Do we offer our children and our lives?
Faithful waiting in old age; the elderly as witnesses of hope.
Joy and sorrow together: the Child is the sign that will be opposed.
Present yourself to God as Lent begins.
live: Offer your day
Begin each morning this week by presenting your day to God.
Honour the elderly
Visit an elderly person and listen to their memories of faith, as Simeon and Anna would have shared theirs.
Pray Simeon's song
Pray Luke 2:29–32 each night before sleep.
fathers: St Sophronius of Jerusalem
“Let us all hasten to meet him… let us all carry lights… Simeon took him in his arms; let us too embrace him” (Sermon on the Hypapante).
St Ephrem the Syrian
He marvels that the Lord of the Temple was carried into the Temple, and that the old man held the Ancient of Days, who released him in peace (Hymns on the Nativity).
magis: Catechism 529
The presentation of Jesus in the Temple shows him to be the firstborn Son who belongs to the Lord; Simeon and Anna recognise in him the long-expected Messiah.
Catechism 583
Jesus showed deep respect for the Temple, where he was presented forty days after his birth.
Vita Consecrata (on 2 Feb)
The feast of the Presentation is kept in the universal Church as the World Day for Consecrated Life.
saints: 3 Feb: Mar Simon and Morth Hanna (Simeon and Anna). 4 Feb: St John de Britto. 7 Feb: Kothine Sunday; the Great Fast begins.
2027-02-02.prayer: Lord God, your Son was presented in the Temple and received by Simeon and Anna. Accept the offering of our lives; let us wait for you with their faith and welcome you with their joy, and let your Christ be the light of our homes and of all nations. Amen.

2027-02-07.title: Kothine Sunday · First Sunday of the Great Fast
readings: Return to me with all your heart
Is not this the fast that I choose?
In Antioch they were first called Christians
2027-02-07.alt: Kothine Sunday, the miracle at Cana: first Sunday of the Great Fast. The special prayers of the Fast begin this evening; Shubkono, the service of reconciliation, is on Monday 8 February.
2027-02-07.verse: Jesus did this, the first of his signs, in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
theo: The Malankara Church begins the Great Fast with a wedding. On Kothine Sunday we read the miracle at Cana, where Jesus changed water into wine. It may seem strange to start a season of fasting at a feast, but it is deeply wise. The Fast is not about sadness; it is about transformation. The water of our ordinary, tasteless lives can become the wine of God's joy, if we do what Mary says: “Do whatever he tells you.”

The prophets tell us what kind of fast God wants. Joel: “Return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; rend your hearts and not your clothing.” Isaiah: “Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of injustice… to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house?” Fasting from food is meant to open our hearts to God and our hands to the poor.

St Paul shows the inner work of Lent: “Put to death whatever in you is earthly… clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience… Above all, clothe yourselves with love.” The Fast is a change of clothes: putting off the old self and putting on Christ. Acts reminds us that it was in Antioch, the mother Church of our Syriac tradition, that the disciples were first called Christians.

The jars at Cana were filled “up to the brim” with water at Jesus' word. In these fifty days, let us fill our jars: with prayer, fasting, almsgiving and the Word of God. At the end of the Fast, at Qyomtho, Christ will give us the best wine, kept until now: the joy of his Resurrection.
conn: Water into wine.
At Cana water for purification becomes the wine of the wedding feast; the old covenant is fulfilled in the new (John 2:6–10).
The rainbow.
Genesis 9:13: God's covenant after the flood. Lent is a time to return to the covenant God never breaks.
The commandments.
Exodus 20: Lent is a time to examine our lives by the commandments and make a good Confession.
The true fast.
Isaiah 58:6–7 and Joel 2:12–13: fasting with the heart and with the hands.
altar: At Cana Jesus changed water into wine; at the altar he changes wine into his own Blood. Every Holy Qurbono of the Fast is a small Cana, preparing us for the great feast of the Resurrection.
outline: Why does our Lent begin at a wedding?
Water into wine: God changes ordinary lives.
Mary's advice for the whole Fast.
Joel 2 and Isaiah 58: return with the heart, share with the poor.
Prayer, fasting, almsgiving, Scripture; Shubkono and Confession.
live: Make a Lenten plan
Decide as a family: one food to fast from, one daily prayer, one work of charity.
Come to Shubkono
Take part in the service of reconciliation on Monday and ask forgiveness of those you have hurt.
Share your bread (Isaiah 58:7)
Put aside the money saved by fasting for the poor.
fathers: St Ephrem the Syrian
He sings of the Lord who at Cana changed water into wine, and asks him to change our hearts in the same way during the Fast (Hymns on the Fast and on Virginity).
St John Chrysostom
“Do you fast? Give me proof of it by your works… If you see a poor man, take pity on him; if you see an enemy, be reconciled with him” (Homilies on the Statues 3).
magis: Catechism 1434–1439
Interior penance is expressed in fasting, prayer and almsgiving; Lent is a privileged time for it.
Catechism 2043
The precept of fasting and abstinence prepares us for the liturgical feasts.
Catechism 1613
Jesus' presence at Cana confirms the goodness of marriage; the Church sees in it the sign of the new covenant.
saints: 8 Feb (Monday): Shubkono; the Great Fast begins. 10 Feb: anniversary of the establishment of the Syro-Malankara Major Archiepiscopate (2005). 11 Feb: Our Lady of Lourdes, World Day of the Sick.
2027-02-07.prayer: Lord Jesus, at Cana you changed water into wine and revealed your glory. As we begin the Great Fast, change our hearts: teach us to do whatever you tell us, to fast with love, to share with the poor, and to reach with joy the feast of your Resurrection. Amen.

2027-02-14.title: Garbo Sunday · The Healing of the Leper
readings: Naaman is cleansed in the Jordan
They shall seek the Lord their God
Jesus touches and cleanses a leper
2027-02-14.alt: Second Sunday of the Great Fast.
2027-02-14.verse: Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.
theo: The Sundays of the Great Fast in our tradition follow Christ the physician: the leper, the paralytic, the Canaanite woman's daughter, the bent woman, the man born blind. Lent is a season of healing. Today a man “covered with leprosy” falls on his face before Jesus and says: “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.” Jesus “stretched out his hand, touched him, and said, ‘I do choose. Be made clean.’ Immediately the leprosy left him.”

Leprosy in the Bible was more than a disease. The leper had to live outside the camp, cry “Unclean!”, and could touch no one. Jesus does what no one would do: he touches him. The Law said that touching a leper made you unclean; with Jesus, the opposite happens: his touch makes the leper clean. This is what Lent offers us: the touch of Christ on the parts of our life we hide from others.

Naaman, the proud Syrian general, was told by Elisha to wash seven times in the Jordan. At first he was angry: was this not too simple? But when he obeyed, “his flesh was restored like the flesh of a young boy, and he was clean.” Healing requires humility. The leper in the Gospel knelt; Naaman went down into the river. In Lent we kneel in confession and go down into the waters of repentance.

Isaiah prays: “O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in the time of trouble.” Jesus himself, after healing the leper, “would withdraw to deserted places and pray.” Healing and prayer go together. Let us bring to Christ in this Fast whatever in us is unclean, and hear him say: “I do choose. Be made clean.”
conn: Naaman and the leper.
Elisha healed a foreigner through the waters of the Jordan; Jesus heals with a touch and a word. Jesus himself recalls Naaman (Luke 4:27).
The ark.
Noah entering the ark (Genesis 7) is an image of salvation through the Church and Baptism (1 Peter 3:20–21).
Outside the camp.
Leviticus 13:45–46 excluded lepers; Christ “suffered outside the city gate” (Hebrews 13:12) to bring the excluded in.
Sin as leprosy.
The Fathers saw leprosy as an image of sin: it spreads, isolates and disfigures; only Christ cleanses.
altar: The leper asked to be touched; in Holy Communion Christ does more than touch us: he enters us. Before Communion we say with the centurion and the leper: Lord, I am not worthy, but only say the word.
outline: The Sundays of Lent: Christ the physician.
Humble, trusting prayer. Jesus always chooses to heal what we bring him.
Jesus touches the untouchable. Who are the “lepers” of our society?
Healing through simple obedience: Confession, prayer, fasting.
Jesus withdrew to pray; make space for prayer in Lent.
live: Make a good Confession
Bring Christ what you hide most; hear the words of absolution as his touch.
Touch the untouchable
Visit or help someone avoided by others: a patient, a migrant worker, a prisoner's family.
Morning prayer (Isaiah 33:2)
Begin each day of the Fast with “O Lord, be our arm every morning.”
fathers: St John Chrysostom

Christ touched the leper to show that he was not under the law but above it, and that to the pure nothing is impure: his hand did not become unclean, but the leprous body became clean (Homilies on Matthew 25).
St Ephrem the Syrian
He calls Christ the Physician who came down to the sick, and asks that the medicine of his mercy heal the hidden sores of the soul (Hymns on the Fast).
magis: Catechism 1503–1505
Christ the physician: his compassion for the sick and his healings are signs that God has visited his people; he takes up our infirmities.
Catechism 1421
The Lord Jesus, physician of our souls and bodies, willed that his Church continue his work of healing in the sacraments of Penance and Anointing.
Message for the World Day of the Sick
The Church cares for the sick as Christ did; read the Pope's annual message (11 February) on vatican.va.
saints: The weekdays of the Great Fast. 22 Feb (next Monday): the Throne of St Peter at Antioch.
2027-02-14.prayer: Lord Jesus, physician of souls and bodies, you touched the leper and made him clean. Stretch out your hand over us in this Fast: cleanse what is hidden, heal what is wounded, and give us the humility of Naaman and the faith of the leper. Amen.

2027-02-21.title: M'shario Sunday · The Healing of the Paralytic
readings: The song of Moses as a witness
They hear your words but do not do them
Woe to those who call evil good
Signs and wonders by the apostles
While we were still sinners, Christ died for us
Four friends lower the paralytic through the roof
2027-02-21.alt: Third Sunday of the Great Fast.
theo: Jesus is teaching in a crowded house in Capernaum. Four men bring a paralysed friend on a mat, but they cannot get near. So they climb onto the roof, dig through it, and lower him down in front of Jesus. Mark says: “When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’” The faith of the friends opens the way for the sick man.

Everyone expected a healing of the legs. Jesus begins with the heart. The deepest paralysis is sin: it keeps us from walking towards God and towards others. The scribes object: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” They are right; and that is exactly the point. Jesus then says: “So that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins… stand up, take your mat and go to your home.” The visible healing proves the invisible one.

Ezekiel warns of people who listen to the prophet's words like a lovely song and do nothing: “they hear what you say, but they will not do it.” Isaiah cries: “Ah, you who call evil good and good evil.” The paralysis of the soul often begins there: hearing without doing, calling sin by softer names. Lent is the time to stand up and walk.

St Paul gives the reason for our hope: “God proves his love for us in that while we still were sinners Christ died for us.” We do not have to cure ourselves first. Like the paralytic, we only need to be brought to Jesus, and to let others carry us when we cannot walk.
conn: Carried by faith.
The four friends are an image of the Church: we carry one another to Christ by prayer, intercession and example.
Authority to forgive.
Christ gave this authority to the apostles (John 20:22–23); it continues in the sacrament of Penance.
Hearing and doing.
Ezekiel 33:32 and James 1:22: be doers of the word, not hearers only.
Peter's shadow.
Acts 5:15: the sick are laid on mats in the street so Peter's shadow may fall on them; Christ's healing continues through the Church.
altar: At every Holy Qurbono we are like the paralytic, lowered before the Lord by the prayer of the whole Church. Before Communion the priest prays for the forgiveness of our sins; then the Lord says to us, “Stand up and walk.”
outline: The roof broken open: what would we do to bring a friend to Jesus?
Point 2 · Sin is the deepest paralysis
Ezekiel and Isaiah: honesty about sin.
Confession and a new start; God loved us while we were sinners.
live: Carry a friend
Pray every day this week for one person who cannot or will not come to God.
Do what you hear (Ezekiel 33:32)
Choose one teaching from today's Gospel and act on it this week.
Confession
If you have not yet confessed this Lent, do it this week.
fathers: St Ambrose of Milan
How great is the Lord, who for the merit of some pardons others… If you doubt your own merit, seek the prayers of others; the Church will pray for you (Exposition of the Gospel of Luke 5, 11).
St Ephrem the Syrian
He sees in the paralytic the human race, made helpless by sin, which the Physician raised by a word, showing that he who forgives is God (Commentary on the Diatessaron).
magis: Catechism 1441–1442
Only God forgives sins; Jesus, the Son of God, exercises this divine power and gives it to his apostles for the Church.
Catechism 1421
Christ, physician of souls and bodies, healed the paralytic and forgave his sins; the Church continues this in Penance.
Catechism 2634–2636
Intercessory prayer: asking on behalf of another, as the four friends did.
saints: 22 Feb: the Throne of St Peter at Antioch. 23 Feb: St Polycarp of Smyrna. 24 Feb: the Finding of the Head of St John the Baptist. 25 Feb: Blessed Rani Maria (as in the 2025–26 lectionary).
2027-02-21.prayer: Lord Jesus, you saw the faith of four friends and forgave the sins of the paralytic. Forgive our sins, heal the paralysis of our hearts, and make us friends who carry others to you. Raise us up, that we may walk in your ways. Amen.

2027-02-28.title: Knanoitho Sunday · The Canaanite Woman
readings: Thus far the Lord has helped us
A house of prayer for all peoples
2027-02-28.alt: Fourth Sunday of the Great Fast. The middle day of the Fast falls on Wednesday 3 March, when the Cross is erected in the church.
2027-02-28.verse: Woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.
theo: A Canaanite woman, a foreigner and a pagan, comes shouting after Jesus: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is tormented by a demon.” At first Jesus does not answer her. The disciples want her sent away. Jesus says he was sent to the lost sheep of Israel. But she kneels and says: “Lord, help me.” And when Jesus speaks of the children's bread, she replies: “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table.”

This is one of the most moving prayers in the Gospel. She does not argue about her rights; she does not give up; she accepts being called small, and still trusts. Jesus is amazed: “Woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.” Her daughter is healed from that hour. Jesus' silence was not a refusal; it was a school of persevering faith.

Isaiah had prophesied that foreigners who hold fast to the covenant would be brought to God's holy mountain, “for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.” The Canaanite mother is the first fruit of that promise. The bread meant for the children is enough for all; in the desert God “rained bread from heaven” for the whole people (Exodus 16:4).

St Paul cries out in Romans: “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” The mother's cry and Paul's cry are the same: we cannot save ourselves, but Christ can. Halfway through the Fast, the Church sets up the Cross in the middle of the church: the answer to every cry for help.
conn: A house of prayer for all peoples.
Isaiah 56:7, quoted by Jesus when cleansing the Temple, is fulfilled when a Canaanite woman finds mercy.
Crumbs and the bread from heaven.
The manna (Exodus 16) and the multiplication of loaves just before and after this Gospel (Matthew 14–15) point to the Eucharist, offered to all nations.
Ebenezer.
Samuel's stone “Thus far the LORD has helped us” (1 Samuel 7:12) is the grateful memory of persevering faith.
Pride and humility.
Sirach 10:12–13: pride begins when we forsake the Lord; the woman's humility opens heaven.
altar: The woman asked only for crumbs from the table. At the Holy Qurbono we receive not crumbs but the whole Bread of Life. Let us come with her humility: “Lord, I am not worthy.”
outline: When God seems silent: do we give up?
Silence, refusal, and still she kneels: “Lord, help me.”
She accepts being small and trusts anyway.
Isaiah 56: God's house is for everyone; welcome the stranger.
Mid-Lent: the Cross set up in our church; renew your Lenten resolutions.
live: Don't stop praying
Take up again a prayer you abandoned because God seemed silent.
Pray for your children
Mothers and fathers: bring each child's needs to Jesus by name, like the Canaanite mother.
Welcome a stranger
Show kindness to someone of another background, language or faith this week.
fathers: St John Chrysostom
Christ delayed the gift not to drive her away but to reveal her faith; her persistence made her an example to all the ages (Homilies on Matthew 52).
St Ephrem the Syrian
He praises the mother whose love for her daughter made her bold, and whose humility drew mercy from the Lord of the table (Commentary on the Diatessaron).
magis: Catechism 2610
Jesus teaches filial boldness in prayer: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you receive it.” He is amazed at the faith of the Canaanite woman.
Catechism 2742–2745
Persevering prayer; praying without ceasing.
Catechism 543
Everyone is called to enter the Kingdom; announced first to Israel, it is meant for all nations.
saints: 3 Mar (Wednesday): the middle day of the Great Fast; erection of the Cross (Gogultho). 7 Mar: K'piphtho Sunday. 9 Mar: the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste.
2027-02-28.prayer: Lord Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on us. Give us the humble, persevering faith of the Canaanite mother; hear our prayers for our children and families; and make your Church a house of prayer for all peoples. Amen.

quick: The Lord enters his Temple in Mary's arms.
Simeon: “My eyes have seen your salvation.”
Joy and the sword: the Child will give himself for us.
2027-02-02.action: Present your day to God each morning this week.
2027-02-02.question: Have I presented my life, my family and my work to God?
2027-02-02.special: Mayaltho, the Entrance of our Lord into the Temple. World Day for Consecrated Life in the universal Church.
illus: Old Kerala grandmothers often say: “I only want to see my grandchildren baptised and receive Holy Communion, then the Lord can take me.” That is Simeon's prayer, prayed in every generation.

family.explain: When Jesus was a baby, Mary and Joseph took him to the Temple. An old man called Simeon held him and was so happy, because he had waited all his life to see the Saviour.
family.intention: We pray for our grandparents and all elderly people, and for sisters, brothers and priests who have given their lives to God.
family.ask: Ask: “How can we offer our family to God this week?”

kidsaint: Two very old people who prayed in the Temple every day, waiting for the Saviour. God let them see baby Jesus before they died. Lesson: keep praying and waiting for God; he keeps his promises.
term: Syriac for “entrance”: the feast of the Entrance of our Lord into the Temple, 2 February, forty days after Yaldo. In the West it is called the Presentation of the Lord.
termMore: Luke 2:29–32, “Now, Lord, let your servant go in peace”, is prayed in many Christian traditions at night prayer, at the end of the day.

quick: Our Lent begins at a wedding: the Fast is transformation, not sadness.
Mary's advice for Lent: “Do whatever he tells you.”
The fast God chooses: return with the heart, share with the poor.
2027-02-07.action: Make a family Lenten plan: one fast, one prayer, one work of charity.
2027-02-07.question: What water in my life do I want Jesus to change into wine this Lent?
2027-02-07.special: Kothine Sunday, first Sunday of the Great Fast. The special prayers of Lent begin this evening; remind the faithful about fasting and abstinence and about Shubkono on Monday.
illus: In many Malankara homes the meat pots are scrubbed clean on the evening before the Fast, and the family begins fifty days of simpler food. The clean pots are like the jars at Cana: emptied and ready to be filled with something better.

family.explain: At a wedding in Cana the wine ran out. Mary told the servants: “Do whatever Jesus tells you.” Jesus changed water into the best wine! In Lent Jesus wants to change our hearts too.
family.intention: We pray for a holy Lent for our family, and for people who have no food.
family.ask: Ask: “What will each of us give up this Lent, and what good thing will we do?”

kidsaint: His name means “son of encouragement”. In Antioch he encouraged the new Christians, and brought Paul to teach with him; there the disciples were first called Christians. Lesson: encourage others to be good this Lent.
term: Kothine refers to the wedding at Cana (John 2:1–11). The Malankara Church begins the Great Fast with this Gospel: the Fast is a time of transformation, from water to wine.
termMore: The service of forgiveness (reconciliation) on the first Monday of the Fast. Priest and people ask forgiveness of one another and of God before beginning the fifty days.

quick: Lent is a season of healing: Christ the physician.
Jesus touches the untouchable and makes him clean.
Healing needs humility: kneel like the leper, wash like Naaman.
2027-02-14.action: Make a good Confession during this week of the Fast.
2027-02-14.question: What “leprosy” in my life am I hiding from Jesus?
2027-02-14.special: Garbo Sunday, second Sunday of the Great Fast.
illus: Kerala once had leprosy hospitals run by religious sisters, who washed and bandaged patients whom even their families had abandoned. Visitors were amazed that the sisters touched them with bare hands. They had learnt it from Jesus.

family.explain: A man with a skin disease called leprosy was alone; nobody would touch him. He asked Jesus for help, and Jesus touched him and healed him.
family.intention: We pray for the sick, and for people who are left alone or rejected.
family.ask: Ask: “Who is lonely at school or at work, and how can we be kind to them?”

kidsaint: A Belgian priest who went to live with people suffering from leprosy on the island of Molokai, cared for them, built homes and a church, and finally caught the disease himself. Lesson: love the people others avoid.
term: Garbo is Syriac for “leper”. The second Sunday of the Great Fast, when the Church reads the healing of the leper. The Sundays of the Fast are named after Christ's healings.
termMore: The Malankara Great Fast follows Christ the physician from Sunday to Sunday: the leper, the paralytic, the Canaanite woman's daughter, the bent woman and the man born blind. Lent is our journey of healing towards Easter.

quick: Four friends carry the paralytic to Jesus: we carry each other by faith.
Jesus heals the deepest paralysis first: sin.
Don't only hear the Word; do it.
2027-02-21.action: Pray daily this week for one person who is far from God.
2027-02-21.question: Whom am I carrying to Jesus, and who is carrying me?
2027-02-21.special: M'shario Sunday, third Sunday of the Great Fast.
illus: When a young man in a Kerala parish was bedridden after an accident, his prayer group came every Friday evening, carried him to the car and took him to the adoration chapel. He says their faith kept his alive. They were the four friends of Capernaum.

family.explain: Four friends carried a man who could not walk to Jesus. The house was full, so they made a hole in the roof! Jesus forgave his sins and healed him.
family.intention: We pray for people who cannot walk or are sick in bed, and for friends who are far from God.
family.ask: Ask: “How can we help a friend to come closer to Jesus?”

kidsaint: A Franciscan Clarist sister from Pulluvazhy in Kerala who worked for poor village families in Madhya Pradesh and was killed in 1995. Her killer later repented, and her family forgave him. Lesson: love and forgiveness can heal hearts.
term: M'shario refers to the paralytic, the man who was “loosed” and raised up. The third Sunday of the Great Fast reads his healing (Mark 2:1–12).
termMore: On the weekdays of the Great Fast the Malankara tradition prays with prostrations (kneeling and bowing to the ground), a bodily sign of repentance. They are not made on the Fortieth Friday and on feast days, as the lectionary notes.

quick: Persevering prayer: when God seems silent, keep asking.
Humble faith wins mercy: “even the dogs eat the crumbs.”
God's house is a house of prayer for all peoples.
2027-02-28.action: Take up again a prayer you stopped because God seemed silent.
2027-02-28.question: Have I given up asking God for something important?
2027-02-28.special: Knanoitho Sunday, fourth Sunday of the Great Fast. Announce the middle day of the Fast (Wednesday 3 March) and the erection of the Cross.
illus: A Kerala mother prayed for twenty years for her son who had left home and faith. Every Sunday she lit a candle before Mary. When he came back one Easter, he said: “I knew someone was praying.” The Canaanite woman still lives in our parishes.

family.explain: A mother whose daughter was very sick kept asking Jesus for help, even when he did not answer at first. Because she kept trusting, Jesus healed her daughter.
family.intention: We pray for all mothers and fathers who are worried about their children.
family.ask: Ask: “What do we need to keep asking Jesus for as a family?”

kidsaint: Kidnapped as a child in Sudan and sold as a slave, she later came to know Jesus in Italy, became a sister, and forgave those who had hurt her. Lesson: God's love is for everyone, from every nation.
term: Knanoitho means “the Canaanite woman”. The fourth Sunday of the Great Fast reads the healing of her daughter (Matthew 15:21–28; Mark 7:24–30).
termMore: On the Wednesday after this Sunday, the twenty-fifth day of the Fast, the Malankara Church marks the middle of the Great Fast; the Cross (Gogultho) is solemnly set up in the church, recalling the bronze serpent lifted up in the desert (Numbers 21:9; John 3:14).

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, forty days after Yaldo, Mary and Joseph carry the Child to the Temple in Jerusalem. They come to present him to the Lord, as the Law of Moses required, and they offer two young pigeons, the offering of poor families. The Lord of the Temple enters his own house, carried in his mother's arms.

An old man is waiting there: Simeon, righteous and devout, who had been promised that he would not die before seeing the Messiah. He takes the Child in his arms and sings: “Now, Lord, you are letting your servant go in peace, for my eyes have seen your salvation.” A whole lifetime of prayer is rewarded in one moment. And the old prophetess Anna gives thanks and speaks of the Child to everyone.

But Simeon also says to Mary: “A sword will pierce your own soul too.” The Child presented today will one day offer himself on the Cross. Hebrews tells us that Christ entered the true Holy Place with his own blood, obtaining eternal redemption. The joy of Christmas already carries the shadow of the Cross.

On Sunday the Great Fast begins. Let us do what Mary and Joseph did: present ourselves to God, our families, our work, our whole life. Let us learn from Simeon and Anna to wait for the Lord faithfully. And every time we receive Holy Communion, let us say with Simeon: “My eyes have seen your salvation.” Amen.
kids: Children, when Jesus was a tiny baby, Mary and Joseph took him to the big Temple to give him to God.
An old man called Simeon was there. He had waited all his life to see the Saviour. He held baby Jesus in his arms and said: “Now I am happy; I have seen God's salvation!”
When you receive Jesus or pray to him, you can be happy like Simeon. Let's say: “Jesus, you are my light!”

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today our Church begins the Great Fast, and it begins it at a wedding. On Kothine Sunday we read how Jesus, at Cana, changed water into wine. Why begin fifty days of fasting with a wedding feast? Because the Fast is not a season of gloom. It is a season of transformation.

At Cana the wine ran out. Mary noticed and said to the servants: “Do whatever he tells you.” That is the best advice for Lent. The servants did a simple thing: they filled the jars with water, up to the brim. And Jesus changed that water into the best wine. In this Fast, let us fill our jars: with prayer, with fasting, with the Word of God, with works of mercy. And let Jesus change the water of our lives into wine.

The prophets tell us what true fasting is. Joel says: “Return to me with all your heart; rend your hearts and not your clothing.” Isaiah says: “Is not this the fast that I choose: to share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house?” Fasting from food is not a diet; it makes room in our hearts for God and in our hands for the poor.

Tonight the special prayers of the Fast begin, and tomorrow we celebrate Shubkono, when we ask forgiveness of one another. Let each family make a simple plan: one fast, one prayer, one act of charity. And at the end of these fifty days, at Qyomtho, Jesus will give us the best wine, kept until now: the joy of his Resurrection. Amen.
kids: Children, today Lent begins! And our Gospel is about a wedding party. At the party the wine ran out. Mary said: “Do whatever Jesus tells you.”
The servants filled six big jars with water, and Jesus changed it into wonderful wine! In Lent Jesus wants to change us too: to make us kinder, more patient, more prayerful.
What can you give up this Lent? Sweets? Television? And what good thing can you do? Let's say: “Jesus, change my heart!”

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, in our tradition every Sunday of the Great Fast shows us Christ the physician. Today a leper comes to him. In those days a leper lived outside the village, had to cry “Unclean!” when anyone came near, and could touch no one. This man kneels and says: “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”

Then Jesus does something no one else would do. He stretches out his hand and touches him. “I do choose. Be made clean.” By the Law, touching a leper made a person unclean. But with Jesus the opposite happens: his touch makes the leper clean. That is what Lent offers each of us: the touch of Christ on the part of our life we hide from everyone.

Our first reading tells of Naaman, a proud Syrian general with leprosy. The prophet told him simply to wash seven times in the Jordan. He was offended: is that all? But when he humbled himself and obeyed, his flesh became like a child's. Healing needs humility. For us, the Jordan is the sacrament of Confession. It seems too simple. But it heals.

After healing the leper, Jesus withdrew to deserted places to pray. Let us make room for prayer in this Fast, make a good Confession, and reach out to the “lepers” of our time: the sick, the lonely, those everyone avoids. And let us hear Jesus say to us: “I do choose. Be made clean.” Amen.
kids: Children, long ago people with a skin disease called leprosy had to live alone. Nobody would touch them or play with them.
One day a man with leprosy came to Jesus and said: “If you want, you can heal me.” Jesus touched him and said: “I want to. Be healed!” And he was healed!
Is there someone at school whom nobody plays with? Be kind to them, like Jesus. Let's say: “Jesus, make me kind!”

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, imagine the scene in Capernaum. Jesus is teaching in a house so crowded that no one can get to the door. Four men arrive carrying a friend who cannot walk. What do they do? They climb onto the roof, dig a hole, and lower their friend down right in front of Jesus. They would not give up.

St Mark says: “When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’” Their faith. Sometimes we cannot bring ourselves to God; others must carry us. And sometimes we are called to carry others: a son who has left the Church, a friend in addiction, a neighbour in despair. Our prayer can open the roof.

Everyone expected Jesus to heal the man's legs. He began with his sins. The deepest paralysis is not in our legs but in our hearts: sin keeps us from walking towards God and others. Only God can forgive sins, said the scribes. Exactly. And to show that he has that authority, Jesus told the man: “Stand up, take your mat and go home.”

Ezekiel warns of people who hear God's word like a beautiful song and then do nothing. Let us not be like that this Lent. Let us make a good Confession, so that we hear Jesus say: “Your sins are forgiven.” And let us become the four friends who carry others to him. Amen.
kids: Children, four friends wanted to bring their friend who could not walk to Jesus. But the house was full of people!
So they climbed onto the roof, made a hole, and lowered their friend down on a mat right in front of Jesus! Jesus forgave his sins and said: “Stand up and walk!” And he walked!
Good friends help each other come to Jesus. Let's say: “Jesus, help me to be a good friend!”

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today a mother comes to Jesus. She is not one of his people; she is a Canaanite, a foreigner. Her daughter is suffering terribly. She cries out: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David!” And Jesus does not answer her a word.

Have you ever felt that? You pray and pray, and heaven seems silent. The disciples even want her sent away. Jesus says he was sent first to Israel. But she does not give up. She kneels and says three simple words: “Lord, help me.” And when Jesus speaks of the children's bread, she answers with amazing humility: “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table.”

Jesus is amazed: “Woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.” His silence was not a refusal. It was a school of faith, and she passed with honours. Isaiah had said that God's house would be a house of prayer for all peoples. This foreign mother shows us that no one is outside God's mercy.

This Wednesday we reach the middle of the Fast, and the Cross is set up in our church. Look at it when you feel God is silent. St Paul cries: “Who will rescue me? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” Mothers and fathers, keep praying for your children. Don't give up. Say with her: “Lord, help me.” Amen.
kids: Children, a mother came to Jesus because her daughter was very sick. She asked and asked: “Jesus, please help!” At first Jesus did not answer.
But she kept trusting and asking. Jesus said: “Your faith is great!” And her daughter was healed.
When you pray and nothing seems to happen, don't stop! Jesus is listening. Let's say: “Jesus, help me!”

intro: Theme: “The Lord comes to his Temple.”
Forty days after his birth, Mary and Joseph bring Jesus to the Temple. There two elderly people, Simeon and Anna, recognise him. The Lord whom Israel sought has come to his house.

sub: The Law allowed those who could not afford a lamb to offer two birds.
Mary and Joseph bring the offering of the poor; yet they carry the true Lamb.
God values not the size of our gift but the heart that offers it.
q: If she cannot afford a sheep, she shall take two turtledoves or two pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering.
They offered a sacrifice according to what is stated in the law of the Lord, “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”
points.apply: Offer yourself, your family and your work at the altar today, however small it seems.

sub: Malachi promised: the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple.
Simeon, righteous and devout, waited for the consolation of Israel; the Spirit led him to the Child.
Holding Jesus, he sings: now I can depart in peace. Faithful old age sees salvation.
q: The Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple.

Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel.
points.apply: Honour the elderly in your family and parish; listen to their faith.

points.h: A sign that will be opposed
sub: Isaiah spoke of a stone of stumbling as well as a sanctuary.
Simeon tells Mary that the Child will be a sign opposed, and a sword will pierce her soul.
Following Christ means choosing a side; Mary shows us how to stand faithful in sorrow.
q: He will become a sanctuary, a stone one strikes against; for both houses of Israel he will become a rock one stumbles over.

This child is destined for the falling and the rising of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be opposed so that the inner thoughts of many will be revealed—and a sword will pierce your own soul too.
points.apply: Ask Mary for courage to remain faithful to Christ when it costs you.

concl: The Light of the nations entered the Temple in the arms of his mother.
Let us receive him as Simeon did, and let our lives be an offering in his house.
2027-02-02.resolve: Pray Simeon's song (Luke 2:29–32) each night before sleep this week.

intro: Theme: “The Fast begins at a wedding.”

Our Great Fast does not begin with ashes but with a wedding at Cana. The Church tells us that Lent is not sadness but the joyful return of the Bride to the Bridegroom, who turns the water of our efforts into the wine of his grace.

sub: Joel calls: return with fasting, weeping and mourning; rend your hearts, not your clothing.
At Cana Mary notices: “They have no wine.” Lent begins by admitting what we lack.
Her counsel is the programme of the Fast: “Do whatever he tells you.”
q: Yet even now, says the LORD, return to me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning; rend your hearts and not your clothing.
When the wine gave out, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.” … His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”
points.apply: Name the “wine” that has run out in your life (joy, peace, love) and bring it to Jesus.

sub: Fasting from food has meaning when it frees us for justice and charity.
Isaiah: share your bread, shelter the homeless, clothe the naked.
Jesus: fast in secret; the Father who sees in secret will reward you.
q: Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of injustice, to undo the thongs of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free … Is it not to share your bread with the hungry?
But when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face, so that your fasting may be seen not by others but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
points.apply: Set aside the money saved by fasting for the poor.

sub: The servants fill the jars to the brim; Jesus does the rest.
The best wine is kept for last: God's grace exceeds our efforts.
After the flood God gave a covenant sign; at Cana Jesus gives the first sign of the new covenant.
q: I have set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.
“You have kept the good wine until now.” Jesus did this, the first of his signs, in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him.
points.apply: Fill your “jars” this Lent: daily prayer, Scripture, fasting and charity, and trust Jesus to transform them.

concl: The Fast is a wedding feast in preparation: the Bridegroom is coming to his Passion and Resurrection.
Let us return with all our hearts, fast as God desires, and let him change our water into wine.
2027-02-07.resolve: Choose three Lenten practices (prayer, fasting, almsgiving) and write them down today.

intro: Theme: “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”

The Great Fast leads us through Sundays of healing. The first is the leper: a man shut out of community, who dares to come to Jesus. Leprosy is an image of sin, which isolates us from God and from one another.

sub: The Law made the leper live alone, outside the camp.
Sin does the same: it breaks our communion with God, family and Church.
The leper does not hide; he falls on his face before Jesus and asks.
q: He shall remain unclean as long as he has the disease; he is unclean. He shall live alone; his dwelling shall be outside the camp.
There was a man covered with leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he bowed with his face to the ground and begged him, “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”
points.apply: Name the sin that isolates you, and bring it humbly to the Lord.

sub: No one touched lepers; Jesus stretches out his hand and touches him.
His answer is clear: “I do choose.” God wants our healing.
The Psalmist knows the connection: “heal me, for I have sinned against you.”
q: As for me, I said, “O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you.”
Then Jesus stretched out his hand, touched him, and said, “I do choose. Be made clean.” Immediately the leprosy left him.
points.apply: Reach out this week to someone others avoid: the sick, the shamed, the lonely.

sub: Naaman wanted a dramatic cure; he was told simply to wash in the Jordan.
When he obeyed, his flesh became like a child's.
Jesus sends the healed man to the priest: today Christ heals our sins through the priest in Confession.
q: So he went down and immersed himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of the man of God; his flesh was restored like the flesh of a young boy, and he was clean.
“Go,” he said, “and show yourself to the priest, and, as Moses commanded, make an offering for your cleansing, for a testimony to them.”
points.apply: Make a good confession during this Great Fast.

concl: What the leper said, we can say: “Lord, if you choose, you can make me clean.”
Christ chooses. Let us come to him, let him touch us, and go home clean.
2027-02-14.resolve: Prepare an examination of conscience this week and go to confession.

intro: A paralysed man cannot reach Jesus by himself. Four friends carry him, break open a roof and lower him down. Jesus sees their faith, forgives the man's sins and raises him up.

sub: Aaron and Hur held up the weary hands of Moses until the battle was won.
Four friends carry the paralytic and find a way through the roof.
The Church is a community where we carry one another to Jesus by prayer and help.
q: Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side; so his hands were steady until the sun set.
And when they could not bring him to Jesus because of the crowd, they removed the roof above him; and after having dug through it, they let down the mat on which the paralytic lay.
points.apply: Carry one person to Jesus this week: pray for them by name and help them practically.

sub: Jesus first says: “Son, your sins are forgiven.” The deepest paralysis is sin.
The Psalmist blesses God who forgives all iniquity and heals all diseases.
In the sacrament of Reconciliation Christ still speaks these words through his priest.
q: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and do not forget all his benefits—who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases.
When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.”
points.apply: Thank God for the times he has forgiven you, and forgive someone who has hurt you.

sub: God takes no pleasure in the death of the sinner, but wants him to turn and live.
Jesus shows his authority: “Stand up, take your mat and go to your home.”
The healed man walks out before all; forgiveness gives new life and new strength for daily duties.
q: As I live, says the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from their ways and live.
“I say to you, stand up, take your mat and go to your home.” And he stood up, and immediately took the mat and went out before all of them.
points.apply: Take up one duty you have been avoiding at home, and do it with new heart.

concl: Faith carried the man, mercy forgave him, power raised him.
Let us be friends who carry others, sinners who accept forgiveness, and disciples who rise and walk.
2027-02-21.resolve: Pray each day this week for one person who is spiritually or physically “paralysed”.

intro: A foreign mother cries out for her daughter. Jesus is silent; the disciples want her sent away; she is answered with a hard word. Yet she persists, and Jesus praises her great faith. Her story teaches us how to pray when God seems silent.

sub: She is a Canaanite, an outsider, yet she calls Jesus “Lord, Son of David”.
She brings her daughter's suffering as her own: “Have mercy on me.”
Isaiah's prayer is hers and ours: “O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you.”
q: O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in the time of trouble.
Just then a Canaanite woman from that region came out and started shouting, “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is tormented by a demon.”
points.apply: Pray this week for children in trouble: sick, addicted, lost or far from God.

sub: “He did not answer her at all.” God's silence is not his absence.
The Psalmist also cried: “How long, O LORD?”
She does not leave; she kneels: “Lord, help me.” Persistent, humble prayer grows deeper through testing.
q: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?
But he did not answer her at all … But she came and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, help me.”
points.apply: Do not stop praying for the intention you have carried longest.

points.h: Great faith and bread for all
sub: She accepts the hard word humbly and turns it into hope: even the dogs eat the crumbs.
Jesus praises her: “Woman, great is your faith!” and her daughter is healed.
Isaiah foresaw it: foreigners gathered into God's house of prayer for all peoples.
q: These I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer … for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.
She said, “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table.” Then Jesus answered her, “Woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.”
points.apply: Welcome a stranger or someone from another community in your parish or workplace.

concl: The Canaanite woman shows us humble, persistent, confident faith.
Let us keep praying for those we love, and never doubt that the Lord's table has bread for all.
2027-02-28.resolve: Pray a decade of the Rosary each day this week for a child or young person in difficulty.
